text: The Taliban released a biography of reclusive leader Mullah Mohammed Omar to dispel rumors of his death and assert his authority. The document aims to reaffirm his leadership amid growing competition from ISIS. Omar has not been seen or heard from in years, fueling speculation about his fate.

Hundreds of mourners attended the funeral of Walter Scott, a black man fatally shot by a white police officer in South Carolina, calling his death a catalyst for change. The service highlighted racial tensions and calls for reform, as Officer Michael Slager faces murder charges. Scott's death, captured on video, has sparked national debate over police conduct and racial injustice.

A former TSA agent was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly videotaping a female co-worker in a bathroom and burglarizing her home. Daniel Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and computer violations, receiving probation and GPS monitoring. The TSA confirmed Boykin was terminated and held no public screening role.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to drive economic growth, lacking traditional natural resources. The government and private sector are promoting music through festivals and industry events to boost tourism and global exposure. This strategy aims to capitalize on the nation's cultural wealth to foster long-term development.
Arsenal defeated Burnley 1-0 to stay four points behind Premier League leaders Chelsea. Meanwhile, Aston Villa beat Tottenham 1-0, while Sunderland suffered a 4-1 home defeat to Crystal Palace.

Original "Twin Peaks" cast members launched a #SaveTwinPeaks video campaign backing David Lynch amid his salary dispute with Showtime. Lynch exited the upcoming revival Sunday, citing insufficient funding to execute the scripts properly. Showtime stated it continues to hope the reboot proceeds with both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Andrew Getty, 47, heir to the Getty oil fortune, was found dead in his Los Angeles home. Police suspect natural causes, citing prior health issues, and say no foul play or criminal investigation is underway. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the exact cause of death.

The mother of a quadriplegic man left in a Philadelphia park for days cannot be extradited from Maryland until she completes unspecified treatment. Nyia Parler, 41, faces charges including aggravated assault for allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old son, who was found suffering from dehydration and other injuries. The man was discovered in Cobbs Creek Park after his mother reportedly left him to visit her boyfriend in Maryland.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Malala Yousafzai, honoring the Pakistani education activist. Asteroid 316201 Malala, discovered in 2010, orbits between Mars and Jupiter. Mainzer said the recognition highlights the need for girls' education to solve global challenges.

Nearly 100 people aboard the Celebrity Infinity cruise ship have fallen ill with a gastrointestinal sickness, the CDC reports. The cause of the outbreak, which has affected 95 passengers and five crew members, remains unknown. CDC officials will board the vessel in San Diego to investigate.

The "Star Wars" saga launched on digital HD and "Dukes of Hazzard" actor James Best died. Mindy Kaling's brother revealed he faked being black for medical school, and a couple named Burger-King got a free wedding. Nina Dobrev announced her "Vampire Diaries" exit and Michelle Obama danced at the White House Easter egg roll.

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman with attempting to travel overseas to fight for ISIS, one of three women arrested this week on terror-related charges. Keonna Thomas, 30, allegedly purchased a ticket to Spain as a cover before planning to enter Syria via Turkey. Two New York women were also arrested for allegedly plotting attacks in the U.S.

HBO released a teaser for season 2 of "True Detective," starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch. The new season follows three law-enforcement officers and a career criminal entangled in a California murder conspiracy. The critically acclaimed series premieres June 21.

Authorities have charged Carlos Colina, 32, after human remains were found in a duffel bag and an apartment building in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The victim was identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who knew the suspect. Colina faces charges of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury and improper disposal of a body, with additional charges possible.

A Kentucky high school basketball star asked a freshman with Down syndrome to prom, a gesture that went viral. Trey Moses surprised Ellie Meredith with flowers and a Taylor Swift-themed poster during her P.E. class. The act was praised by their school and community, highlighting the importance of inclusion.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week sequel to the hit miniseries, following the early days of Christianity. Other notable premieres include the final episodes of "Mad Men" and the launch of Marvel's "Daredevil" on Netflix. The week also sees new series like "American Odyssey" and the return of "Louie" on FX.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed a controversial religious freedom law to shore up conservative credentials for a potential 2016 White House run, drawing widespread backlash but gaining support among the GOP's right wing. The resulting furor is dragging the entire Republican presidential field farther right, forcing candidates to address a wave of similar state-level anti-LGBT bills. Despite national progress on gay rights, conservatives' focus on "religious freedom" legislation threatens to make cultural warfare a central issue in the 2016 election.

Apple's latest iOS update introduces diverse emojis, adding varied skin tones and same-sex couple options. The expanded inclusivity draws mixed reactions, drawing conservative criticism while leaving some groups, like redheads and Armenians, demanding further representation.

Singer Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease after a tick bite last spring. The 30-year-old, now 80 percent better, is releasing a new single this month and says the illness gave her a new perspective on life.

New research by the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and Margot Frank died at least a month earlier than previously believed, likely in February 1945. Researchers cited typhus symptoms and camp conditions to contradict the prior March 31 death date determined by Dutch authorities.

Two Alabama college students were arrested and charged with gang raping a woman during spring break in Panama City, Florida. The incident was discovered after police found video of the assault during an unrelated investigation. Both students have been suspended from Troy University, and more arrests are expected.

A Washington State dog survived being hit by a car, struck with a hammer, and buried alive, later staggering to a farm for help. The one-year-old bully mix, named Theia, is recovering from severe injuries with support from a foster owner and public donations. The case echoes a similar survival story of a cat in Florida.

The FBI has confirmed the death of wanted terrorist Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, during a January raid in the Philippines. Marwan was killed in a botched operation that left 44 Philippine police commandos dead. The mission has been criticized for jeopardizing a fragile peace agreement with a major rebel group.

Critics argue the Iran nuclear deal concedes too much, allowing Tehran to keep its nuclear infrastructure and receive sanctions relief while lacking robust inspection safeguards. They warn the agreement risks empowering a state sponsor of terrorism and could enable Iran to develop a nuclear weapon, echoing past failures with North Korea. The deal is seen as a strategic loss, giving up leverage that could have forced Iran to dismantle its program.

AMC's "Mad Men" begins its final season Sunday, closing out the 1960s era it has deeply influenced. As the old advertising order disintegrates, characters face likely exits from the newly McCann Erickson-owned firm. Creator Matthew Weiner remains tight-lipped, but the series is expected to conclude with Don Draper facing a changing world alone.

A giraffe named Katie at the Dallas Zoo gave birth live on the Internet early Friday evening. The newborn, about 6 feet tall, showed promising signs like moving its ears and attempting to stand. The zoo announced the birth on Twitter, though the calf's gender and condition were not immediately confirmed.

Loretta Lynch's nomination for attorney general faces an unprecedented Senate delay, longer than the previous eight nominees combined. While some cite partisan disputes, others allege racial bias is a factor in the prolonged wait. The historic nomination of the first African-American woman to the post remains in limbo.

Armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in northern Afghanistan's Balkh province, killing three and wounding five. Afghan security forces remain engaged in an ongoing firefight with the attackers as they cautiously advance to avoid civilian casualties.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to host "The Price Is Right" for the first time since his 2007 retirement. The TV legend led the April 1 episode's opening game before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration linked to his Type II diabetes but has since returned home to rest. His daughter and publicist confirmed he is feeling much better and recovering with family. King, known as the "King of the Blues," has a history of similar health issues, including dehydration last year.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev's Boston Marathon bombing conviction highlights the need to understand Muslim radicalization, which stems from political grievances rather than the religion itself. Extremists exploit real-world crises to recruit young Muslims, offering violence as a false solution. Countering this requires addressing these grievances and demonstrating that extremism harms, rather than helps, the global Muslim community.

Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion is becoming a church. North Carolina's Carowinds debuts the Fury 325, the world's tallest and fastest giga-coaster. A CNN exclusive details sexual assault allegations against Bikram yoga founder Bikram Choudhury.

The Pentagon reports coalition forces have reclaimed 25-30% of ISIS-held territory in Iraq. A counterinsurgency expert cautions that these frontal gains do not signify a turning tide, noting ISIS strategically withdraws to launch diversionary attacks elsewhere to maintain its image. He criticized the coalition's conventional push, advocating for maneuverist warfare to disrupt ISIS supply chains.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight to Atlanta was allegedly choked with a headphone cord by another traveler. The suspect was met by U.S. authorities and taken for a medical evaluation, with no federal charges currently filed. The victim, a professional soccer player, was aided by other passengers and is reportedly unharmed.

Former British banker Rurik Jutting was charged with two counts of murder after the bodies of two Indonesian women were found in his Hong Kong apartment. One victim was discovered on the floor, while the other was hidden in a suitcase on the balcony. A court hearing to determine if the case will proceed to trial has been adjourned until May.

A massive tornado outbreak struck the Midwest Thursday, killing one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and destroying dozens of homes. A large twister cut a 22-mile path through Ogle County, flattening structures and trapping residents, though early warnings limited casualties. Severe weather, including additional tornadoes and large hail, threatened the region as cleanup efforts began.

Don McLean's 16-page manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's. The sale marks the third-highest auction price for an American literary manuscript. McLean, 69, said he parted with the draft to provide for his family.

UNRWA chief Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit to Syria's Yarmouk refugee camp Saturday to assess the humanitarian crisis. ISIS and Al-Nusra control roughly 90% of the camp, leaving 18,000 trapped civilians facing severe malnutrition and aid shortages.

A Saudi-led coalition's airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen have killed hundreds and devastated infrastructure, leaving millions without power or clean water. The Red Cross warns of a humanitarian catastrophe and urges a ceasefire, while the UN Security Council has failed to act. The conflict, rooted in regional power struggles, has also allowed al Qaeda to exploit the chaos.

Former Australian cricket captain and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at 84 after a battle with skin cancer. A legendary figure, he was a record-breaking player and later cricket's most iconic commentator. Tributes poured in globally, with leaders and players hailing him as the voice and soul of the sport.

A nearly five-minute total lunar eclipse, the shortest of the century, is visible for western North America. The eclipse began at 3:16 a.m. PDT, with totality occurring at 4:58 a.m. PDT. A partial eclipse is visible across the U.S., though sunrise will interrupt the view on the East Coast.

Millionaire heir Robert Durst has been federally charged with unlawful firearm possession, adding to his legal troubles. He faces a first-degree murder charge in California for the 2000 killing of Susan Berman and could face the death penalty. Durst, who was featured in the HBO documentary "The Jinx," also faces state weapons and drug charges in New Orleans.

"Furious 7" premieres Friday, featuring a rewritten script and touching on-screen tribute to late star Paul Walker. Walker's character was retired rather than killed off, with his brothers serving as body doubles to complete his scenes. Co-star Vin Diesel and fans worldwide continue to mourn the actor, whom many praised for his quiet off-screen generosity.

A "Price Is Right" model accidentally revealed the correct price for a new car, prompting host Drew Carey to award the prize. The contestant won the Hyundai Sonata, and the model later tweeted that everything was fine. The incident followed an appearance by former host Bob Barker.

Thai Smile Airways has unveiled an Adventure Time-themed Airbus A320, featuring characters like Jake and Finn on its exterior and interior. The partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone includes themed headrests and air sickness bags. The inaugural flight from Bangkok to Phuket is scheduled for April 4.

Pedestrians in downtown Washington, D.C., stopped traffic and used an umbrella to herd a mother duck and her ducklings across a busy street. The bystanders safely guided the birds to an enclosed grassy area after the animals caused a stir on L Street NW.

French investigators have completed evidence collection at the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site, securing the area with private security. The flight data and cockpit voice recorders were recovered, along with 150 DNA profiles and 470 personal effects. Authorities confirm co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane, killing all 150 aboard.

Cuba and the U.S. are attending the Summit of the Americas together for the first time since 1962, marking a historic thaw in relations. The two nations are negotiating to restore diplomatic ties and re-open embassies, though Cuba demands removal from the U.S. terrorism list first. Street clashes between Cuban government supporters and dissidents in Panama underscore ongoing tensions despite the diplomatic progress.

Jesus and his disciples funded their ministry through donations from wealthy supporters, including women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna. These followers provided from their own resources, making the mission viable. The ministry operated at a subsistence level, relying on hospitality and contributions.

California regulators have ordered Pacific Gas & Electric Co. to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe operations, including the 2010 San Bruno pipeline explosion that killed eight people. Most of the penalty will fund pipeline safety improvements. PG&E apologized and said it is working to enhance safety.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old basketball player who inspired millions with her fight against brain cancer, has died. She fulfilled her dream of playing college basketball and raised $1.4 million for cancer research. Hill is remembered as a symbol of courage and determination.

A large fire broke out at a General Electric industrial park in Louisville, Kentucky, Friday morning. Authorities reported no injuries and worked to contain the blaze, whose cause remains unknown. The fire prompted a multi-alarm response.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, a key negotiator in the nuclear talks, has a lesser-known past including U.S. education and a federal investigation. Despite a hero's welcome at home, his biography contains conflicting details about his age. Zarif continues to work closely with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry to finalize the agreement by a June 30 deadline.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to release 17-year-old "Cassandra C." from state custody, despite her being in remission after nearly six months of forced chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. The state retains custody, viewing her as a flight risk after she previously ran away from treatment. She is expected to return home once her final round of chemotherapy concludes at the end of April.

New psychological computer analysis confirms the 1728 play "Double Falsehood" was primarily written by William Shakespeare and John Fletcher, with negligible contribution from publisher Lewis Theobald. Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin identified the authors' distinct linguistic signatures, showing Shakespeare wrote the first half while Fletcher shared the second. Despite the scientific findings, some literary scholars doubt the centuries-old authorship debate will be fully settled.

The French prosecutor denied any video from Germanwings Flight 9525 was used in the investigation, disputing reports by two magazines. The publications claimed to have seen a cell phone video showing the plane's final moments. Meanwhile, Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had informed them of a previous severe depression episode during his training.

Decorated veteran Emy Afalava, born in U.S. territory American Samoa, is denied citizenship despite the 14th Amendment. He and other American Samoans are suing to challenge this last remaining exception to birthright citizenship. A federal court ruling is pending.

Blue Bell shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant after listeria was found in ice cream produced there. The CDC warned consumers not to eat products from the facility, which is linked to a listeria outbreak that sickened five and killed three in Kansas. The company issued its first-ever recall as investigations into the contamination continue.

Al-Shabaab claimed an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya, killing many and taking hostages. The Somalia-based group, linked to al-Qaeda, has escalated cross-border raids since 2011, exploiting regional instability. The attack underscores worsening security in East Africa amid broader political and socioeconomic challenges.

The U.S. has lodged a formal complaint with Russia after a Russian SU-27 fighter jet intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in an "unsafe and unprofessional" manner. The Pentagon stated the incident occurred in international airspace, while Russia claimed the U.S. aircraft was flying with its transponder off. This follows a similar dangerous close pass between the two nations' aircraft last year.

A hooded black angel artwork appeared near where Walter Scott was fatally shot by a North Charleston police officer. Creator Phillip Hyman crafted the reclaimed wood piece to mourn Scott's death and reflect on racial injustice. Black Lives Matter protesters have since adopted the figure as an icon for their demonstrations outside City Hall.

A North Charleston police officer has been fired and charged with murder after a bystander's video showed him shooting an unarmed man, Walter Scott, as he fled. The footage contradicts the officer's initial report that Scott had taken his Taser. The witness who recorded the video disputes the officer's account of the struggle.

ISIS claimed to have seized part of Iraq's largest oil refinery at Baiji, posting images of the assault online. Iraqi officials denied the claim, stating their forces remain in full control of the strategic facility. The reports could not be independently verified.

Nashville's district attorney banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, a practice used four times in five years. The article argues such voluntary deals are likely constitutional but have sparked outrage due to gender bias, as similar offers to male offenders are less controversial. The practice remains morally and legally debated.

Over 25,000 people have contracted Ebola in the past year, with more than 10,000 deaths, leaving survivors and global health systems permanently altered. While weekly cases have fallen to their lowest since May 2014, Guinea reports ongoing transmission risks from unsafe burials and undetected cases. The WHO warns that unknown chains of transmission could spark new infections despite progress in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

The NCAA claims it has no legal duty to ensure the academic integrity of courses for student-athletes, contradicting its public stance that education is paramount. The position was taken in response to a lawsuit over a massive academic fraud scandal at the University of North Carolina. Critics accuse the organization of hypocrisy and abandoning its core responsibilities.

An explosion at a controversial paraxylene plant in Zhangzhou, China, injured six people and sparked a major fire, now under control. The blast followed an oil leak at the facility, which was relocated from Xiamen in 2007 following pollution protests.

A defense attorney argues the fatal shooting of Walter Scott proves police body cameras are essential to ensure accountability and prevent tragedies. While acknowledging body cameras are only an interim fix for systemic racial bias in law enforcement, he asserts they immediately reduce use-of-force incidents and help restore public trust.

The anticipated U.S.-Cuba rapprochement at the Summit of the Americas was overshadowed by a "triangle of tension" involving Venezuela. Venezuelan President Maduro accused the U.S. of plotting a coup, prompting sanctions and a diplomatic firestorm. Cuba, Venezuela's key ally, publicly condemned the U.S. and sided with Maduro, complicating the summit for Washington.

A fire broke out on a nuclear submarine at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard during welding repairs. The blaze, involving rubber hull insulation, poses no threat as nuclear fuel, ammunition, and hazardous materials were previously unloaded. All personnel evacuated safely with no injuries reported.

Downgraded tropical storm Maysak, locally named Chedeng, approaches the Philippines with 70 mph winds, prompting flood and landslide warnings. Authorities have barred coastal activities, ordered precautionary evacuations, and turned away tourists in vulnerable areas. The storm is expected to make landfall Sunday morning in Isabela province before exiting by Monday.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly rebuked his son, Deion Jr., on Twitter for claiming to eat only "hood doughnuts." The elder Sanders reminded his son of his trust fund, condo, and clothing line, telling him to "stop the hood stuff." Deion Jr. appeared to take the public scolding in stride, retweeting his father's comments.

Guatemala faces an epidemic of gender-based violence, with high femicide rates fueled by a legacy of war, impunity, and deep-rooted misogyny. Despite new laws and grassroots efforts to empower women, a weak justice system and pervasive machismo leave millions at risk. International attention and immediate action are urgently needed to combat the crisis.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring residents to photograph their cattle and submit details to a database to enforce a new beef ban. The measure follows a state-wide prohibition on cow slaughter, which carries a five-year prison sentence. Over 100 owners have complied as authorities aim to prevent illegal killings of the revered animals.

Lucknow police are deploying pepper-spraying drones to control violent protests and mob attacks. The four purchased drones, costing up to $19,300 each, will also carry cameras for surveillance. Critics warn the measure suppresses free speech and reflects authoritarian policing over dialogue.

The original handwritten lyrics to Don McLean's iconic 1971 song "American Pie" sold at auction for $1.2 million. The 16-page manuscript was purchased by an unnamed buyer at a Christie's auction. The song, a cultural anthem reflecting on 1950s and 60s America, remains one of the most celebrated compositions of the 20th century.

A daring London vault heist over Easter echoes old-school robberies, with meticulous planning and likely inside help. Police are pursuing a relentless investigation, focusing on forensic evidence and criminal networks. The motive remains purely financial, with thieves targeting easily convertible goods like cash and jewelry.

7-Eleven is hosting its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day Saturday, allowing customers to fill any sanitary container for $1.49. The promotion, which runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., kicks off peak Slurpee season with size restrictions enforced by in-store displays. The event is separate from the chain's annual Free Slurpee Day on July 11.

Former Kentucky State Senator Georgia Powers condemns Rand Paul's presidential bid, arguing his record on civil rights and voting rights contradicts his claims of inclusion. She asserts his positions would take the country backward and are disqualifying for the presidency.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at Walt Disney World Speedway during the Exotic Driving Experience, killing a 36-year-old passenger. The 24-year-old driver lost control and sustained minor injuries. Operator Petty Holdings extended sympathies following the fatal Sunday accident.

The defense in the Aaron Hernandez murder trial rested its case in less than a day after prosecutors spent months presenting 131 witnesses. Key evidence includes Hernandez's alleged lie to his boss about the murder time and disputed testimony about a footprint and a gun seen on video. The jury will now begin deliberations in the circumstantial case.

Chinese authorities have detained five women's rights activists for "creating disturbances" ahead of a legal deadline that could lead to formal arrest. The detentions, targeting prominent feminist organizers, coincide with China's push for new anti-domestic violence legislation and the 20th anniversary of the Beijing women's conference. Activists face increased scrutiny as the government cracks down on independent civil society groups.

Former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley challenged Hillary Clinton's "inevitability" for the Democratic nomination, arguing frontrunners often falter. Speaking in Iowa, O'Malley called for a robust primary contest despite polling at just 1%. Clinton is expected to announce her candidacy Sunday.

Former NFL player Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison for the 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd. The victim's family delivered emotional impact statements, remembering Lloyd as a devoted family man and forgiving his killer. The verdict concluded a painful two-year ordeal for Lloyd's mother and relatives.

Presidential candidate Ted Cruz is courting Iowa's influential evangelical base, emphasizing his faith and social conservatism. He aims to unite religious, tea party, and libertarian voters to secure a crucial early victory. Cruz's strategy includes highlighting religious liberty issues and deploying a pastoral campaign style to energize this key demographic.

Marvel Studios revealed Paul Bettany as the Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron" and unveiled the Daredevil suit for the Netflix series. Bryan Singer announced Ben Hardy as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse," while a new look at The Thing from "Fantastic Four" was also released. The flurry of reveals underscores the continued dominance of superhero content.

Nearly 1,000 migrants were rescued off Libya's coast Friday, as Italy reports over 10,000 arrivals this year. Most flee Africa and the Middle East, with 480 deaths recorded so far, a sharp rise from last year. Smugglers often use overcrowded, unsafe vessels, abandoning passengers at sea.

French global TV network TV5Monde regained partial control Thursday after a cyberattack disrupted its 11 channels and social media. The attack, claimed by an Islamist group with ISIS logos appearing, left the network scrambling to restore operations. One channel and its Facebook page were back online, though some websites remained under maintenance.

Director David Lynch has exited the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient network funding. Showtime expressed regret over his departure but stated the nine-episode third season will move forward without him.

Major court trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev are concluding in Massachusetts, while Sen. Rand Paul announced his presidential bid in Kentucky. Chicago faces a mayoral runoff and Ferguson holds elections under the shadow of last year's protests.

Tornadoes touched down in Kansas and Missouri overnight, with reports of damage and flooding. The storms, which included baseball-sized hail, are expected to continue Thursday across the Midwest and Mississippi River Valley. Nighttime tornadoes were highlighted as particularly dangerous.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. The judge imposed the maximum sentence after two juries deadlocked on the death penalty. Arias expressed remorse before the sentencing, while Alexander's family delivered emotional victim impact statements.

The EPA found the restricted pesticide methyl bromide in a luxury U.S. Virgin Islands villa where a Delaware family fell ill. The family was hospitalized after exposure, which may have resulted from a nearby fumigation. The incident is under investigation by the EPA and the Department of Justice.

An outside review found Rolling Stone's retracted UVA rape story was an "institutional failure" of reporting and editing. The magazine apologized for the damage caused. While the university cannot sue, fraternity members may have a viable defamation case if they can prove individualized harm.

FBI agents shot and captured an armed robbery suspect in Georgia after a chase that left two agents injured in a crash. The suspect, Kevone Charleston, was wanted for 32 commercial robberies and was wounded but is expected to survive. The incident ended a lengthy investigation into his crimes.

An Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle after a ramp agent fell asleep in the cargo hold. The pilot heard banging, prompting an emergency landing 14 minutes after takeoff. The employee was unharmed, and the flight later continued to Los Angeles.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks is eligible for the death penalty if convicted in the February shooting deaths of three Muslim college students. Hicks, who was indicted on three first-degree murder counts, claimed a parking dispute motivated the killings, while victims' families and federal authorities are investigating potential hate crime charges.

Amnesty International reports that women's rights activists in Afghanistan face increasing attacks from the Taliban, warlords, and government officials, with little protection from authorities. The report highlights the brutal murder of Farkhunda and the subsequent protests, where women defied tradition by serving as pallbearers. Despite the dangers, activists continue their fight for rights, urging the government and international partners to protect them.

A New York judge authorized serving divorce papers to a defendant entirely via Facebook private message. The ruling modernizes alternate service methods, offering a more reliable and trackable option than antiquated legal fictions like service by publication or "nail and mail." As defendants increasingly evade traditional process servers, courts are recognizing that people are now easier to locate online than at a physical residence.

The Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" television ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, has died at age 88. The California televangelist, known for his "possibility thinking" message, had been diagnosed with esophageal cancer in 2013. His ministry later faced financial decline and bankruptcy after a succession struggle.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a fire on a Pemex oil rig off Mexico's coast. The blaze, which has been extinguished, prompted the evacuation of about 300 people. Pemex denied reports the platform collapsed and said there was no oil spill.

Kansas has enacted the first U.S. law banning a common second-trimester abortion procedure, which it defines as "dismemberment abortion." The measure, signed by Gov. Sam Brownback, allows exceptions to protect the mother's life or health. Supporters call it a groundbreaking step, while opponents warn it is dangerous and among the most restrictive abortion laws in the country.

Chinese state TV host Bi Fujian sparked controversy after a video showed him cursing late Chairman Mao Zedong at a private dinner. Bi later apologized, and his employer, CCTV, announced an investigation into the incident. The incident has divided public opinion in China, where disrespect for leaders remains taboo.

University of Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for a racial slur he muttered about Wisconsin player Frank Kaminsky after a loss. Harrison, who is black, said the comment about the white player was made in jest and has since apologized to Kaminsky. Kaminsky accepted the apology and said the matter was resolved.

"Arrested Development" will return for a 17-episode fifth season, executive producer Brian Grazer confirmed. Netflix declined to comment, and it remains unknown if the original cast will reprise their roles.

The Large Hadron Collider has restarted after a two-year shutdown, with beams circulating in its 17-mile ring. Scientists aim to recreate conditions after the Big Bang to uncover the universe's mysteries, including dark matter and the origin of mass. The LHC will soon operate at record energy levels to probe fundamental physics questions.

An Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, raising concerns about potential escalation. U.S. officials suspect the unsafe maneuver was locally ordered, possibly indicating a lack of full control by Iranian commanders. The incident occurred amid ongoing nuclear talks and regional tensions.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was convicted on all 30 counts for the Boston Marathon bombing, including 17 capital charges. The trial now moves to the penalty phase, where the same jury will decide whether he receives the death penalty. Jurors will weigh aggravating factors against mitigating ones, including his age and brother's influence.

Four employees of Indian retailer FabIndia were arrested after a minister discovered a security camera aimed at a store changing room in Goa. The staff face voyeurism and privacy charges, while the store's manager remains at large. FabIndia is cooperating with the investigation.

Iran will lift its decades-old ban on women attending some men's sports events, starting with indoor competitions, a top sports official announced. The move follows international pressure, including from FIFA, over the restrictions deemed un-Islamic since the 1979 revolution. The policy change will not apply to all matches, as authorities claim some sports are not of interest to families.

Satyam Computers founder Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in prison and fined for India's largest corporate fraud. Raju admitted in 2009 to inflating profits by $1.6 billion with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

A woman with cancer was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii for lacking a doctor's note, causing her to miss chemotherapy. The airline later apologized, refunded her tickets, and covered accommodations, admitting the situation could have been handled better. The removal was prompted by concerns over her well-being on a long-haul flight.
Beloved Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan died of cancer in Istanbul at 66. Best known for his love songs, he battled the disease since 1990 and performed his final concert on Valentine's Day.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the Iran nuclear deal, calling for increased pressure to secure a better agreement. Netanyahu argued the pact leaves Iran's nuclear infrastructure intact and cannot be trusted, while U.S. officials defended it as a viable alternative to conflict. The deal has sparked partisan debate in Washington, with Republicans largely opposing it and Democrats urging support.

Two connected shootings in Washington began with a domestic kidnapping incident, authorities said. A guard was critically wounded at the U.S. Census Bureau headquarters before the suspect fled, leading to a chase and shootout that injured an officer and the suspect. The kidnapping victim was found safe.

Imprisoned WikiLeaks source Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating posts via phone due to a prison internet ban. Manning, serving 35 years for the largest classified leak in U.S. history, is also receiving authorized hormone therapy for gender dysphoria.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on felony drug charges after a traffic stop revealed methamphetamine, marijuana, and drug paraphernalia on his tour bus. Authorities also found several handguns and packaging materials. Nelly was jailed but later released on bond.

A Delaware family fell critically ill during a US Virgin Islands vacation after suspected exposure to methyl bromide, a restricted toxic pesticide. The EPA detected the chemical in their rented villa, prompting a DOJ criminal investigation. Rental agent Sea Glass Vacations has terminated its pest control contract with Terminix, whose services are linked to the incident.

Online journalists in Asia face increasing legal and deadly threats as governments and independent actors target them for dissent. Authoritarian regimes use restrictive laws, surveillance, and imprisonment to silence online voices, while weak rule of law leaves bloggers vulnerable to deadly attacks with impunity. The trend shows no sign of abating, with online activity becoming the most dangerous form of journalism in the region.

Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving "The Vampire Diaries" at the end of this season after six years. Fans are demanding the show end with her departure, fearing the continuation of a seventh season will ruin the central romance. Producer Julie Plec supported Dobrev's exit and confirmed the series will continue.

ISIS fighters recently stormed the besieged Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp in Damascus, prompting intense government shelling that has flattened buildings and trapped civilians. Jabhat al-Nusra now controls the district as the attrition war continues, leaving the remaining 18,000 residents without food, water, or medical aid. Despite the devastation, defiant residents refuse to evacuate the decimated camp.

NASA scientists outlined steps to discover life beyond Earth in the coming decades, with the James Webb Space Telescope set to search for biosignatures on exoplanets. While simple life may be common, the odds of finding intelligent, communicative civilizations are slim due to vast time scales and technological challenges. Discoveries of primitive life are likely imminent, but contact with advanced aliens remains improbable.

A 32-year-old Massachusetts man faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag and an apartment building. The victim, 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, knew the suspect, Carlos Colina. Colina, previously charged with assault and improper disposal of a body, is scheduled for arraignment April 14.

Kanye West settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos over a 2013 airport assault. Terms were undisclosed, but included a written apology and a handshake. The settlement averts next week's trial.

President Obama's drive to secure his foreign policy legacy has made the US the desperate party in Iran nuclear talks, yielding a weak framework agreement. The deal allows Iran to keep much of its nuclear infrastructure, lifts sanctions too soon, and fails to stop Tehran's nuclear threshold status. Arab allies view the concession-heavy pact as a win for Iran, fueling regional instability and proliferation fears.

Bystander video led to murder charges against a North Charleston officer for gunning down an unarmed black man, exposing false initial police reports. The case highlights a broader lack of data on police killings, as a 1994 federal law mandating the Justice Department to track excessive force remains unimplemented. Without comprehensive, mandatory reporting, the true scope of police violence across the nation remains unknown.

Five Americans monitored for Ebola in Omaha after exposure in Sierra Leone were released, with none developing the virus. One remains in the area due to a heart issue, while the others returned home. The CDC expects the last of 17 monitored patients nationwide to be released by Thursday.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars tops the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, becoming the decade's longest-leading No. 1 and only the 10th song ever to lead for at least 13 weeks. Natalie La Rose's "Somebody" featuring Jeremih enters the top 10 at No. 10.

Twitter celebrated "Rex Manning Day" on April 8, referencing the 1995 film "Empire Records." The date joins other fictional holidays like "Mean Girls Day" on October 3 and "Back to the Future Day" on October 21, 2015. These dates are popularized by iconic movies and marked by fans online.

Critically panned Nicole Kidman starrer "Grace of Monaco" will bypass U.S. theaters and premiere on Lifetime May 25. The Weinstein Co. sold the film directly to the cable network following poor international performance and prolonged disputes over final cut.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance issuing "partnership certificates" to same-sex couples, granting limited rights like hospital visitation and co-signing tenancies. Though not legally binding and lacking federal marriage benefits, activists hailed the move as a significant first step toward marriage equality in conservative Japan.

California's historic drought is driving up grocery prices nationwide, with significant increases seen in produce, beef, and veal. New state-mandated water restrictions will also alter the tourist experience, requiring restaurants and hotels to curb water usage. However, the dry conditions have yielded one unexpected benefit: a string of high-quality vintages for California wines.

The University of Michigan reversed its decision to cancel a screening of "American Sniper" after a student backlash. The university's vice president called the initial cancellation a mistake inconsistent with free expression. An alternative screening of "Paddington" will be offered for students who object.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards featured highlights including Channing Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez and Amy Schumer's sharp monologue. Misfires included an archery gag gone wrong and a controversial "Gone Girl" joke. The show balanced strong performances with awkward moments.

A 20- to 30-foot fiberglass boat fragment suspected to be from the 2011 Japanese tsunami washed up off the Oregon coast this week. Live yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters were found inside the debris. Biologists deemed the invasive species risk low; the boat will be landfilled while the fish go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

One year after Boko Haram kidnapped nearly 300 schoolgirls in Chibok, Nigeria, most remain missing, feared enslaved or killed. The abduction sparked global outrage under the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, but the militant group still controls territory and continues abductions. Nigeria's incoming president has pledged to combat Boko Haram, while the girls' families endure ongoing grief.

The Easter Triduum, encompassing Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday, marks the Christian progression from crucifixion to resurrection. This three-day pattern reflects the universal human experience of suffering, transition, and renewal. The holiday's focus on spiritual transformation allows it to resist secular commercialization.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to Al-Shabaab suspects following the Garissa university massacre that killed 147. Authorities also launched airstrikes against the militant group's camps in Somalia and offered a bounty for the attack's alleged organizer.

Chinese-American entrepreneur Jia Jiang launched "100 Days of Rejection" to conquer his fear of being turned down, leading to viral fame and his book "Rejection Proof." The project, which began after a failed startup, taught him to embrace rejection as an opportunity. Jiang now shares his experience to help others overcome similar fears.

Attorney General Eric Holder has banned Justice Department personnel from soliciting prostitutes, even where legal, citing links to human trafficking. The directive follows a report on DEA agents attending sex parties funded by cartels. Violators will face suspension or termination.

Authorities are investigating the fatal shooting of a Wayne Community College employee as a possible hate crime. The suspect, a former work-study colleague, was arrested in Florida after fleeing the scene. Investigators are also examining potential ties to a white supremacist gang.

Amnesty International reports a global rise in governments using the death penalty to combat crime and terrorism, despite a lack of evidence it is an effective deterrent. While executions dropped overall in 2014, death sentences spiked sharply, with China remaining the world's top executioner. The group urges nations to abandon the practice, noting 140 countries have already abolished it.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a noose on campus and faces a conduct review after being barred from campus. Police are investigating whether others were involved. The incident prompted hundreds of students and faculty to march in protest against racism.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known for playing Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law," has died at 86. Dysart, who won an Emmy in 1992 for the role, died Sunday in Santa Monica after a long illness. His extensive career also included film roles in "Wall Street" and "The Thing."

Easter's shifting date is determined by the first Sunday after the vernal equinox's full moon, aligning it with Passover and causing Western and Orthodox dates to diverge. Pope Francis marked Holy Week in Vatican City by calling for global peace, while Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulcher hosted Resurrection celebrations. Secular traditions like the Easter bunny and colored eggs originated in 17th-century Germany and can be adapted using Kool-Aid dye.

Comedian Chris Rock highlighted racial disparities in policing by documenting three traffic stops in seven weeks on Twitter. His posts sparked debate, with some praising him for raising awareness and others accusing him of race-baiting. The incident echoes Rock's past comedy sketch on avoiding police mistreatment as a black man.

Lynyrd Skynyrd's original drummer, Robert Lewis Burns Jr., died in a single-car crash in Georgia at age 64. Burns, who was not wearing a seatbelt, was a founding member of the band before leaving in 1975. He was not involved in the 1977 plane crash that killed other band members.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs has sparked social media debate over whether it is going up or down. The image, popularized on 9gag.com, has drawn comparisons to past optical illusions like #TheDress. Advertisers are reportedly capitalizing on the public discussion.

The U.S. and its partners reached a framework agreement with Iran to limit its nuclear program and block it from building a weapon. The deal includes strict inspections and reduces Iran's nuclear capabilities, but faces political opposition. Critics have made several misleading claims about the agreement's objectives and terms.

Rolling Stone retracted a discredited article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia, but the piece highlighted broader issues with the school's handling of sexual assault. UVA has never expelled a student for sexual assault and faces ongoing investigations into its policies. Survivors fear the retraction may discourage others from coming forward, despite the article sparking important discussions.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed outside a New York nightclub, leaving him and two others injured. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction charges while checking on Copeland. A suspect is in custody, and Copeland is in stable condition.

Twisted Sister announced its 2016 farewell tour, "Forty and F*ck It," marking the band's 40th anniversary. Mike Portnoy will replace late drummer A.J. Pero, who died in March. The band will also play two memorial shows honoring Pero.

Scientologist John Travolta dismissed HBO's critical documentary "Going Clear," stating he hasn't seen it and doesn't care to. He defended the Church of Scientology as a positive force in his life, crediting it with helping him through personal tragedy. Travolta attributed the film to disgruntled former members and reiterated his satisfaction with his 40-year involvement.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million opening weekend as fans praised its emotional tribute to the late Paul Walker. Producers retired his character gracefully rather than killing him off, avoiding what the director called an exploitative choice. The poignant farewell, featuring a montage and the song "See You Again," left moviegoers visibly moved.

HBO's "Game of Thrones" premieres its fifth season simultaneously in 170 countries. Major story arcs will converge and surpass George R.R. Martin's books as the series builds toward its end after seven seasons. Expect bigger battles, the common folk's uprising, and key focus on Arya, Sansa, and Cersei.

Recent maritime castaways survived extreme ordeals adrift at sea through rationing, ingenuity, and luck. Survivors include Louis Jordan, rescued after 66 days off North Carolina; Jose Salvador Alvarenga, who drifted across the Pacific for over a year; Ron Ingraham, found after 12 days near Hawaii; and Adrian Vasquez, rescued near the Galapagos after 26 days. Hiromitsu Shinkawa also survived after being swept 15 kilometers out to sea by the 2011 Japanese tsunami.

The first six "Star Wars" films debut on digital HD Friday with exclusive special features. The extras include a rare behind-the-scenes look at the saga's sound effects, such as the creation of alien Geonosian voices.

A federal jury has found Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts. Victims expressed relief but noted the verdict cannot erase their pain. The decision is seen as a step toward closure for the community.

China's former security czar Zhou Yongkang has been formally charged with bribery, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets. Zhou, the highest-ranking official ever to face corruption charges, was a former member of the Politburo Standing Committee. His case is seen as a landmark in President Xi Jinping's anti-graft campaign.

A Philadelphia mother was charged with assault, kidnapping, and neglect after allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for over four days to visit her boyfriend in Maryland. The man, found with severe dehydration and malnutrition, was hospitalized while his mother faces extradition to Philadelphia. Authorities are investigating his prior care despite family members stating they were willing to look after him.

Walmart's opposition to Arkansas' religious freedom law, alongside its wage increases, signals a shift in public opinion on key social issues. The retailer's stance contributed to the governor's decision to amend the bill, highlighting growing business support for gay rights. This corporate backlash reflects broader national trends and pressures on political leaders to adapt.

A lapsed Catholic recounts leaving the faith after a parish rejected her grief-stricken request for a priest, but says Pope Francis' non-judgmental tone has reawakened her belief. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix affirms the Pope's approach, emphasizing that while Church doctrine remains unchanged, its door is open to all sinners without rejection. The author now plans to return to church, inspired by a shift from imposed rules to proposed Gospel.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau, who served prison time for her relationship with student Vili Fualaau, says they remain happily married. The couple, who will celebrate their 10th anniversary, will discuss their relationship in an upcoming interview. Letourneau Fualaau also plans to teach again and seek removal from the sex offender registry.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential bid makes her the de facto barometer for U.S. gender equality, placing an unfair burden on her candidacy. However, extrapolating broader truths about women's electability from her race is flawed, given her unique political baggage and research showing female candidates win at equal rates to men. Ultimately, partisanship and the economy, not sexism, will decide the election's outcome.

Amnesty International reports governments are using the threat of terrorism to justify executions, despite a global decline in their use. While the number of executions fell 22% in 2014, death sentences rose sharply by 28%, often after unfair trials. The organization maintains the long-term trend is toward worldwide abolition.

Japan's defense minister says the Air Self-Defense Force has never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs. Minister Gen Nakatani confirmed fighter jets are scrambled for unidentified objects but only find birds or terrestrial debris. The statement was prompted by a query from former pro-wrestler lawmaker Antonio Inoki.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films drama about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt. Wahlberg is expected to play Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis, with the film told from Davis's perspective. It is the second Boston bombing film announced, following Fox's "Boston Strong."

Democratic presidential hopefuls Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb showcased contrasting campaign styles at an Iowa event. O'Malley actively worked the crowd, while the more reserved Webb engaged selectively. Both face long odds against frontrunner Hillary Clinton, polling in the low single digits.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested in Turkey while allegedly attempting to cross illegally into Syria. The group, detained at the Turkey-Syria border, had British passports, though the reason for their attempted entry was not disclosed. The British Foreign Office is seeking information from Turkish authorities.

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted FedEx on 15 counts, including drug trafficking and money laundering, for allegedly delivering illegal prescription drugs. FedEx argues it is a "common carrier" protected from liability for packages it transports without knowledge of their contents. The case highlights the government's strategy of targeting corporations to disrupt illegal drug supply chains, potentially yielding large fines.

Kenyans used social media to honor the 147 victims of the Garissa University College attack by Al-Shabaab, sharing their stories under the hashtag #147notjustanumber. The assault, which targeted Christians, was Kenya's deadliest since 1998. Authorities identified one attacker as the son of a local official.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers using the country's generous parental leave policy, which offers 480 days with a "daddy months" quota to encourage shared caregiving. Despite incentives, only 12% of couples split the leave equally, though Bavman's work highlights the profound impact on fathers who do. His project aims to showcase these men as relatable role models, capturing both the joys and challenges of hands-on parenthood.

President Obama pledged to maintain Israel's military edge over Iran and defend it against any state attack, amid Israeli criticism of the recent nuclear framework. Obama argued the deal allows verification of Iran's nuclear activities, asserting it is especially crucial if Tehran proves untrustworthy.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act faces backlash over potential anti-LGBT discrimination, but experts say such laws are rarely invoked successfully. Past federal and state RFRA cases have primarily involved religious minorities, including Native Americans seeking eagle feathers, a Brazilian church using a sacramental tea, and a Sikh IRS employee carrying a ceremonial knife.

Five Chinese feminists face up to five years in prison for "disturbing public order" after planning International Women's Day protests against sexual harassment. Their detention has sparked international condemnation, with calls for their release. Prosecutors must decide whether to pursue charges by Monday.

Late Tejano star Selena will be recreated as a digital hologram called "Selena the One." The project, developed by Acrovirt and backed by her family, will release new music and tour in 2018. An Indiegogo campaign launching April 16 seeks $500,000 to fund the effort.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to the co-pilot who deliberately crashed Germanwings Flight 9525, claiming his Iran deal would lead to America's destruction. The comment, posted on Facebook, drew widespread criticism for being inappropriate and divisive. Bachmann has previously urged Obama to bomb Iran's nuclear facilities.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River," widely panned by critics, highlights Detroit's decaying landscape as its focal point. Gosling says he filmed the city's crumbling edifices to expose its nightmare of urban decay while also capturing its resilience and ongoing rebirth. The film receives a limited theatrical release on April 10.

A 19-year-old UK national has been charged with terror offenses after being arrested at Luton airport upon his return from Turkey. Yahya Rashid faces charges of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others in such acts between November and March. He is set to appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe's Vince Neil delivered a widely criticized rendition of "The Star-Spangled Banner" at a Las Vegas Outlaws game. The performance joins a history of controversial national anthems, from Roseanne Barr's "disgraceful" version to Jimi Hendrix's iconic Woodstock take. Performances of the song can make artists national heroes or national disgraces.

Nearly 2,000 graffiti inscriptions by WWI soldiers have been discovered in an ancient underground city near Naours, France. The well-preserved markings, left by troops from Australia, Britain, and the U.S., provide a personal record of soldiers who sought refuge there. The site, recently opened to researchers, is being documented by photographer Jeff Gusky.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court, granting the body jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The move, opposed by Israel and the U.S., paves the way for possible war crimes investigations and subjects Palestinians to potential counter-charges. The ICC had already opened a preliminary examination into the situation.

Anthony Ray Hinton walked free after nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row when prosecutors dismissed murder charges following new firearm evidence. Hinton, who maintained his innocence throughout, condemned the unjust loss of three decades of his life. Advocates cited his case as a textbook injustice driven by race, poverty, and prosecutorial indifference.

Most Americans overlook systemic tax unfairness favoring the wealthy and two-worker marriages due to the psychological boost of receiving average refunds near $3,000. Free filing services exploit this "happy ending" effect, using the promise of refunds to upsell profitable add-on products. Consequently, Tax Day has transformed from a dreaded chore into a spending spree, masking deeper structural flaws.

Jordan Spieth survived a late wobble to take a four-shot lead into the Masters final round. Justin Rose and Phil Mickelson surged into contention at twelve and eleven under, respectively. Rory McIlroy and Tiger Woods both finished six under, failing to significantly close the gap on the leader.

A New York woman has been charged with filing a false instrument for allegedly lying on a 2010 marriage license application. Prosecutors say Liana Barrientos married 10 times as part of an immigration scam, sometimes to multiple men simultaneously. She pleaded not guilty and faces up to four years in prison if convicted.

An Indiana pizzeria faced boycotts and threats after stating it would refuse to cater same-sex weddings, citing religious beliefs. In response, supporters raised over $842,000 for the business through a crowdfunding campaign. The incident highlighted the intense national debate over the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

Mindy Kaling's brother, Vijay Chokalingam, is writing a book about getting into medical school by pretending to be African-American to protest affirmative action. Despite his claims of racial privilege, he only received one admission offer and experienced racial profiling during his ruse. The article notes the irony, as Kaling's own career was launched by an NBC diversity program.

Antarctica has possibly recorded its highest-ever temperature of 63.5F (15.5C) at Argentina's Esperanza Base. The World Meteorological Organization is forming a committee to verify the measurement. The record is being closely monitored by climate change researchers.

The Obama administration abandoned its spring timeline for an Iraqi-led offensive to recapture Mosul, stating there is no set timeframe for the operation. Officials emphasized that retaking the larger, strategically vital city requires significant capacity and patience, despite recent progress against ISIS in Tikrit. Airstrikes continue to target ISIS positions around Mosul, but a full ground assault is not imminent.

Irish betting firm Paddy Power deleted a tweet joking about police violence against unarmed African-American males to promote a soccer match. The company apologized, but faced widespread condemnation on social media. The incident is the latest in a series of controversial publicity stunts by the firm.

Philadelphia police have added attempted murder to charges against Nyia Parler, accused of abandoning her quadriplegic son in woods for days. Parler is in custody in Maryland but cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified treatment. The 21-year-old victim was found suffering from dehydration, malnutrition and a cut.

The man accused of stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul has been charged with attempted murder and assaulting a foreign envoy. Kim Ki-Jong allegedly attacked Lippert over joint U.S.-South Korea military drills, leaving the ambassador with severe injuries. His trial must begin within 14 days of the indictment.

"19 Kids and Counting" star Jill Duggar Dillard gave birth to her first child, a 9-lb, 10-oz son named Israel David. The baby arrived over a week past his due date. Dillard is the first daughter in the reality TV family to become a mother.

"Furious 7" is speeding toward a $135 million-$138 million North American debut, marking the largest opening since fall 2013. The late Paul Walker's final film also earned a record-breaking $60 million internationally in early screenings, tracking for a global weekend approaching $300 million. It is Universal's widest release ever, playing in 4,003 domestic theaters and over 10,500 international screens.

A Secret Service supervisor, Xavier Morales, has been placed on administrative leave after a female employee accused him of assault following unwanted sexual advances. The agency, already reeling from recent scandals, is investigating the incident, which Director Joe Clancy called "very disturbing." The allegations add to a series of high-profile missteps that have plagued the Secret Service in recent months.

Hillary Clinton has announced her 2016 presidential candidacy, bringing extensive experience but facing challenges of authenticity and voter enthusiasm. She must avoid appearing inevitable and instead present a compelling vision to connect with voters. Clinton's campaign will need to address doubts about her trustworthiness, policy positions, and potential liabilities tied to her husband.

The DOJ will begin negotiating with Ferguson to restructure its police department following a damning report on racial discrimination. Recent resignations of the city manager and police chief, coupled with the election of two new Black council members, have shifted the city's leadership. The extent of fundamental reform will depend on continued citizen activism during upcoming negotiations.

Etihad Airways lost a 2-year-old pet cat named Felix after its carrier was damaged during a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York. The cat remains missing at JFK Airport, prompting an investigation and search efforts by the airline and local authorities. The airline expressed regret and is reviewing its pet handling procedures.

A sailor, Louis Jordan, was rescued after 66 days adrift in the Atlantic. His 35-foot sailboat was found by a container ship hundreds of miles from land. Jordan survived a broken mast, multiple capsizes, and dwindling supplies by collecting rainwater and catching fish.
